summaries.example: Imagine a note that says, “This note is not true.” If the note is true, then what it says makes it not true. But if it is not true, then the note’s claim seems to be true. The note traps us in a contradiction. This is called the liar paradox.
summaries.summary: Self-reference happens when something refers to itself. A sentence, picture, book, or computer program might point back to itself. Self-reference can be harmless, but it can also create a paradox—a puzzle whose reasoning seems reasonable yet ends in a contradiction. The liar sentence is the best-known example: it says that it is not true. If we call it true, what it says makes it not true. If we call it not true, its claim seems to become true. The entry explains that similar puzzles arise in language, mathematics, knowledge, and computing. Russell’s paradox concerns a supposed collection of all collections that do not contain themselves. The knower paradox concerns a sentence saying that nobody knows it. Other puzzles use an indirect loop, such as two statements on opposite sides of a postcard that refer to each other. Yablo’s paradox shows that an infinite series of statements can cause a contradiction even without a direct self-reference. These puzzles matter because they reveal limits in simple ideas about truth, sets, knowledge, proof, and computation. Proposed responses include arranging things in well-ordered levels, leaving some statements without a truth value, or allowing some statements to be both true and false. There is no single solution accepted by everyone.
key_ideas: Self-reference is not always a problem. “This sentence is true” refers to itself but does not create the same contradiction.
Paradoxes can concern truth, sets in mathematics, or knowledge.
Different paradoxes can look different while sharing a similar pattern: an object is made to turn back on itself.
Some paradoxes do not use a direct loop. A chain of statements can also create trouble.
Philosophers and mathematicians try to avoid paradoxes by limiting self-reference, using levels, or changing how truth works.
summaries.why_it_matters: These puzzles teach us to inspect rules that seem obvious. They helped thinkers understand why mathematics cannot simply make every imaginable collection into a set, why some truths cannot be captured by one formal system, and why no computer program can always predict whether every other program will stop. They also show that a confusing puzzle can point to an important limit in an idea.

important_terms.definition: When something points to or talks about itself. A sentence, picture, story, or computer program can do this.
A puzzle in which reasoning that seems sensible leads to a contradiction or an impossible result.
A sentence that says of itself that it is not true, creating a conflict about whether it is true or false.
A rule or idea that says what counts as true, belongs to a set, or can be known.

questions_to_think_about: Can you make a sentence that talks about itself without causing a contradiction?
Why is “This sentence is true” different from “This sentence is not true”?
Would putting statements into different levels stop a sentence from talking about itself?
Can a puzzle be useful even when it does not have an easy answer?

summaries.example: Consider two speakers. One says, “Everything the other speaker says about a topic is true.” The other says, “Most of the first speaker’s statements about that topic are false.” In ordinary conversation these remarks may be harmless, but a strict language hierarchy has difficulty assigning them levels: each statement refers to a collection that includes the other. This illustrates why simply banning all indirect self-reference can remove ordinary, non-paradoxical speech as well as problematic cases.
summaries.summary: The entry studies self-reference as a source of paradox across philosophy, mathematics, and computer science. A semantic paradox concerns truth or definability; a set-theoretic paradox concerns sets and membership; an epistemic paradox concerns knowledge or knowability. The liar sentence shows the basic difficulty: applying truth to a sentence that denies its own truth produces a contradiction. Russell’s paradox has an almost parallel form, asking whether the set of all sets that are not members of themselves is a member of itself. Diagonalization generalizes this pattern by constructing an object that differs from each item at a corresponding position. The entry presents a broader inclosure-style structure intended to unify many paradoxes, though whether it captures every case and whether all such paradoxes require one solution remains disputed. Self-reference need not be direct. The postcard paradox creates a two-sentence loop, while Yablo’s paradox uses an infinite, non-cyclic sequence in which each sentence refers only to later ones. This raises the broader issue of non-well-founded reference. The consequences are substantial. Tarski’s theorem shows that a sufficiently strong truth schema cannot consistently be added to the relevant formal setting. Related results concern naive set theory, formal theories of knowability, Gödel’s incompleteness theorem, and the undecidability of the halting problem. Proposed strategies include explicit type or language hierarchies, implicit stratification, partial or many-valued truth, revision theories, fixed-point methods, and paraconsistent approaches. These strategies differ over whether paradoxical sentences should be gaps, gluts, unstable over time, or excluded by restrictions on expression. The entry emphasizes that no final,.
key_ideas: Self-reference is neither necessary nor sufficient for paradox: some self-referential sentences are harmless, and some paradoxes use indirect or even non-self-referential structures.
Semantic, set-theoretic, and epistemic paradoxes often share a common pattern in which a construction both belongs and does not belong to a relevant collection.
Unrestricted comprehension leads to Russell’s paradox, while an unrestricted truth predicate leads to formal inconsistency in the setting described by Tarski’s theorem.
The diagonal lemma provides a formal way to construct sentences that behave as though they refer to their own codes or properties.
Self-reference connects paradoxes with Gödel-style limits on proof and Turing’s undecidability result about predicting whether programs halt.

Solutions weaken or reorganize assumptions: explicit or implicit hierarchies, partial truth, revision processes, paraconsistent logic, or restricted principles. No approach is presented as universally agreed upon.
summaries.why_it_matters: Self-reference exposes the boundaries of formal systems. It explains why ordinary-looking principles about truth, set formation, or knowability cannot all be combined without care. The same structural ideas also underlie results showing that some mathematical statements cannot be settled by a given proof system and that no general algorithm can decide whether every program will halt. Studying these limits clarifies both the power and the unavoidable incompleteness of formal reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A statement, description, or object that refers to itself or to something that ultimately refers back to it.
A seemingly acceptable argument or set of assumptions that yields a contradiction, indicating that some concept or assumption needs examination.
A paradox involving concepts such as truth or definability, rather than membership in mathematical sets.
A paradox involving sets, membership, or the foundations of mathematics, such as Russell’s paradox.
A paradox involving knowledge or knowability, such as a statement claiming that it is not known.
A method of constructing an item that differs from the nth item in the nth position; it appears in several paradoxes and proofs of limitation.
A way to block circularity by organizing languages, sets, or knowledge into levels that refer only to lower levels.
A framework in which a sentence may be neither true nor false, or may be both, instead of having only one classical truth value.

questions_to_think_about: Is a paradox best treated as evidence that a particular concept is defective, or could it show that classical logic needs revision?
Why might a hierarchy that blocks the liar also block harmless statements in ordinary conversation?
What is gained and lost by treating the liar sentence as undefined rather than both true and false?
How does diagonalization connect semantic paradoxes with limits on computation and formal proof?
Can an infinite, acyclic chain create a problem similar to a circular loop? Why might compactness matter here?

summaries.example: Suppose a class website has two posts. Post A says, “Post B is true.” Post B says, “Post A is false.” If A is true, then B is true, which says A is false. If A is false, then B is false, but B says A is false, making B seem true. The two posts form a loop. This is an example of indirect self-reference: neither post needs to name itself directly.
summaries.summary: Self-reference occurs when a sentence, definition, picture, or program refers to itself or to a chain that returns to it. The main philosophical interest comes from paradoxes. In the liar paradox, a sentence says that it is not true. Treating it as true makes it false; treating it as false makes its claim true. But not every self-reference is paradoxical: a sentence saying that it is true, or one accurately describing its own length, need not create a contradiction. The entry groups the puzzles into semantic paradoxes about truth and definability, set-theoretic paradoxes about membership, and epistemic paradoxes about knowledge. Russell’s paradox asks about the collection of all things that are not members of themselves. The paradox of the knower uses a sentence saying that nobody knows it. Although these cases differ, they can share a structure in which an object is forced both into and out of a relevant collection. Diagonalization is a recurring technique for producing such constructions. The entry also distinguishes direct self-reference from indirect reference. A postcard with two mutually referring messages creates a loop, while Yablo’s paradox uses an infinite sequence with no direct loop. This shows that certain non-well-founded patterns may be enough for paradox. The consequences include limits on formal theories of truth, naive set theory, knowledge, mathematical proof, and computation. Possible strategies include explicit type or language levels, implicit hierarchies, partial truth with an “undefined” value, revision procedures, and paraconsistent logics that tolerate some contradictions. These approaches have different costs, and the source notes that no generally accepted solution has settled the subject.
key_ideas: The liar paradox is caused by a sentence that says it is not true, but self-reference alone does not always cause trouble.
Grelling’s, Russell’s, and related paradoxes have different topics but similar contradiction-producing patterns.
Some paradoxes are indirect, and Yablo’s paradox suggests that an infinite one-way chain can be problematic without any loop.
Paradoxes reveal weaknesses in simple ideas about truth, set formation, knowledge, and formal reasoning.
One response is to use levels or types so that a sentence cannot apply a truth rule to itself.
Other responses allow an undefined truth status, permit both truth and falsity in special logics, or revise truth step by step.
summaries.why_it_matters: Paradoxes are not merely clever word games. They test the rules we use to talk about truth, collections, knowledge, and programs. They helped reveal that unrestricted rules can make a formal system inconsistent, and that there are limits to what a proof system or computer can decide. Learning about them encourages careful attention to definitions and to the hidden assumptions behind apparently simple reasoning.

important_terms.definition: Referring to oneself, one’s own words, or something that eventually refers back to the original thing.
A reasoning puzzle that appears to use good assumptions but ends in a contradiction.
A paradox about truth, meaning, or whether a description successfully picks out something.
A paradox about mathematical collections and the relation of being a member of a collection.
A paradox about knowledge or what can be known.
A construction that changes or avoids every item in a list by comparing each item with its matching position.
An organized set of levels, where a statement or object can refer only to suitable lower levels.
A sentence or rule that gets its result by applying a process to its own output or description.

questions_to_think_about: Why does self-reference sometimes produce a contradiction and sometimes remain harmless?
Would a rule that prevents every kind of circular statement be too restrictive for everyday language?
What is the difference between a truth-value gap and a truth-value glut?
Why might a paradox in language matter for mathematics and computer science?
Do you think one solution should work for every kind of paradox? Give a reason.
